record.title: The Headache That Made History: How Lou Gehrig Became the Iron Horse
record.summary: On June 2, 1925, a routine lineup change turned into one of baseball's defining streaks.
record.text: It started with a headache. On June 2, 1925, New York Yankees first baseman Wally Pipp told manager Miller Huggins he wasn't feeling well and asked out of the lineup. Huggins turned to Lou Gehrig, and the rest became history.

record.title: The Luckiest Man on the Face of the Earth
record.summary: On July 4, 1939, a packed Yankee Stadium heard Lou Gehrig say goodbye.
record.text: Gehrig played his last game on April 30, 1939, brought down not by age but by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The Yankees held Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day that July 4th, and a crowd gathered to honor him.

record.credit_line: LGFC Editorial Desk -- compiled from SABR archives.

record.title: A Rule Broken Once: Gehrig's Special Election to Cooperstown
record.summary: The Hall of Fame waived its own waiting period for Gehrig -- something it's done only twice, ever.
record.text: Hall of Fame eligibility normally requires years of waiting after a career ends. On December 7, 1939 -- just 221 days after Gehrig played his final game -- the Baseball Writers' Association of America selected him for Cooperstown.

record.title: Before the Pinstripes: Gehrig's One Afternoon at Columbia
record.summary: A scout's train ride to a college doubleheader changed baseball history.
record.text: Before he was a Yankee, Gehrig was an engineering student at Columbia University on a football scholarship. On April 18, 1923, a scout saw him play and changed the course of baseball history.
